# Lab 06 — Policy semantics and deterministic evaluation

**PART II — Foundations of executable governance**  
*Ch. 7 — Policy Semantics and Deterministic Evaluation*

`intermediate` · about 25 minutes

```bash
nornyx-lab run 06      # run it
nornyx-lab check 06    # prove you got it
```

Why three values and not two, why default-deny makes a rule set total, and the
three ordinary programming habits that quietly destroy reproducible decisions.

## By the end of this lab you will be able to

- Name the four things a policy language must define
- Justify a three-valued decision domain and distinguish approval-required from deny
- Apply default-deny and explain why it makes a rule set total
- Identify the three mechanisms that destroy evaluation determinism

## What the lab does, in order

1. What a policy language must define
2. Three values, not two
3. Default-deny makes the rule set total
4. Determinism, and the three things that destroy it
5. Closed schemas as semantic hygiene

## What `check` proves

Each item is one proposition, written so a machine can settle it.
That is the habit the whole book teaches: a governance claim you
cannot express as a test is not yet a claim.

- all three decision values are reachable
- approval required resolves to allow when the input arrives
- default deny answers requests no rule mentions
- evaluation is deterministic across repetition
- two independently loaded authorizers agree
- time is an input so past decisions stay reproducible
- the top level schema is closed
- the authorizer state is not mutable through a handed out view

## Concepts introduced

- `three-valued decision domain`
- `default-deny`
- `evaluation determinism`
- `closed schema`
- `ambient state`
- `wall-clock time`
